interpretation.Bottom line: A 65+ group is **calmer** (lower neuroticism) and **presents itself more favourably** (higher social desirability) than the panel. Both differences replicate on held-out people and survive redefining the group. On values, money style, reflection, generosity and the hypothetical green choice, treat this group as the population average.
interpretation.Claim ledger:
| Claim | Held-out MAE gain vs population mean | Stable in 5 redefinitions | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lower neuroticism | +13.2% (CI > 0) | 5/5 | **Robust** |
| Higher social desirability (corrected) | +9.3% (CI > 0) | 5/5 | **Robust** |
| Slightly higher green values | +3.2% | 3/5 | Weak |
| Lower cognitive reflection | — | — | **Withdrawn** (CRT scoring artefact; corrected d −0.06) |
interpretation.Why it fits: **Observed.** Both traits move steadily across age bands: neuroticism 3.14 → 2.82 → 2.51 → 2.28; corrected social desirability 5.75 → 5.65 → 6.74 → 7.61. **Interpretation.** This matches published cross-sectional age differences in emotional stability and in socially desirable responding. **Speculation.** Ageing, cohort and self-presentation can't be separated here. Social desirability correlates −0.44 with neuroticism, and adjusting for it shrinks the neuroticism gap from −0.50 to −0.31 SD (CI −0.45 to −0.17): part of the calm is self-description, most is not.
interpretation.Say vs do: In the hypothetical $39 renewable offer, 43% chose renewable when it required switching (n = 49; population 36%) and 55% when it was the default (n = 40; 58%). These are not distinguishable from the population, and on held-out members they predict no better than the population rate.
interpretation.Where it breaks: This describes the group, not its members: a random 65+ member is more neurotic than a random 18–29-year-old 25% of the time. The panel's 65+ adults are online-survey completers, and they are over-represented in the experiments (21% vs 10%).

interpretation.Bottom line: Under-50s with household income below $50k show **higher neuroticism**, the largest robust group difference in the project. It reflects **two** visible facts: youth, and lower income *within* every age band. Do not use this persona for money style (the pre-registered 'more spendthrift' prediction failed) or for responses to a costed green offer (the apparent cost effect did not replicate).
interpretation.Claim ledger:
| Claim | Held-out MAE gain vs population mean | Stable in 6 redefinitions | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Higher neuroticism | +11.2% (CI > 0) | 6/6 | **Robust** |
| Lower social desirability (corrected) | +2.0% (CI includes 0) | 5/6 | Fragile: gone if widened to 18–64 |
| More spendthrift (pre-registered) | ≈0 | — | **Falsified** |
| Higher cognitive reflection | — | — | **Withdrawn** (CRT scoring artefact; corrected d +0.00) |
interpretation.Why it fits: **Observed.** Within each age band, lower-income members are more neurotic (18–29: 3.36 vs 2.99; 30–49: 3.07 vs 2.69; age-adjusted +0.30 SD, CI 0.20 to 0.40). Adding sex and income to age raises neuroticism predictability from R² 0.074 to 0.117. **Interpretation.** This is consistent with the documented link between financial strain and negative affect. **Speculation.** The direction is unknown: strain could raise distress, distress could lower earnings, or health could drive both. Household income may also misclassify students living on parental income.
interpretation.Say vs do: When choosing renewable meant switching, 27% chose it on train (n = 33; population 36%), but 47% did on held-out members (n = 19). A tempting 'budget-constrained idealist' story **failed** the holdout, so no behavioural prediction is offered.
interpretation.Where it breaks: About a quarter of members are calmer than the median panel member. The neuroticism gain is a group-level shift that helps individual prediction by about a tenth.

P3.name: P3_young_never_married
P3.selected_by: pre-registered rule in hypotheses.md H6 (src/personas.py select-p3, train only); top of results/p3_selection.csv

interpretation.Bottom line: P3 was chosen by a pre-registered search rule. Its robust trait, **higher neuroticism**, is the same age gradient P2 shows. Its eye-catching trait, **lower green values**, replicated as a group shift but is **fragile and concentrated in young never-married men**, and helps almost no individual prediction. Treat that trait as a hypothesis. Behaviour cannot be assessed.
interpretation.Claim ledger:
| Claim | Held-out MAE gain vs population mean | Stable in 6 redefinitions | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Higher neuroticism | +14.4% (CI > 0) | 6/6 | **Robust** (shared with P2) |
| Lower green values | +0.7% (CI includes 0) | 3/6 | **Fragile**: see caveat |
| Lower social desirability (corrected) | +1.8% (CI includes 0) | 5/6 | Weak |
interpretation.Sex-composition caveat: P3 is 56% male vs 36% among other 18–29s. Never-married **men**: d −0.40 (−0.59, −0.20), n = 111. Never-married **women**: d −0.12 (−0.32, +0.09), n = 86, not distinguishable. The gap also vanishes without the marital criterion (all 18–29: d −0.11) or at ages 30–49 (d −0.09). It came from a search over about 1,000 candidate groups, so it should be confirmed on new data before use.
interpretation.Why it fits: **Observed.** Among 18–29s, the never-married score 3.25 on green values vs 3.84 for others. The gap persists after adjusting for sex, income and education as main effects (−0.45 SD). **Interpretation.** Marital status mostly marks *who* is in the group: more men, and 21% students. **Speculation (not claimed).** That partnering raises environmental concern; composition and selection explain the data equally well.
interpretation.Say vs do: **Insufficient evidence.** Only 33 members took part in the green experiment (17 and 16 per condition, below the 20-per-condition threshold).
interpretation.Where it breaks: P3 predicts individual green values no better than the population mean. Its neuroticism profile duplicates P2's, so census facts mostly reveal one age axis, not three archetypes.
